q: Did games with smaller crowds coincide with smaller national TV audiences in 2025 and 2026?
title: MLB attendance and national TV audiences, 2025-2026
report:
Yes, games with smaller crowds tended to have smaller national TV audiences, but a crowd that was small for its own park did not clearly mean a smaller audience[1]. Comparing games on the same network, the two moved together (correlation 0.34 in 2025, n = 82, range 0.14 to 0.52; 0.47 in 2026, n = 83, range 0.29 to 0.62)[1]. After comparing each game with its own park's usual crowd, the link mostly disappears (0.16 in 2025, range -0.05 to 0.37; 0.14 in 2026, range -0.08 to 0.34; both ranges include zero)[1]. Across team-seasons, teams with bigger average crowds also had bigger average national TV audiences (correlation 0.52, n = 56, range 0.30 to 0.69), which is consistent with team-level factors such as popularity and market size driving both, though the data does not prove the cause[2].

*Viewership figures are publicly reported and may differ from official Nielsen data. They are the national TV audience, excluding streaming add-ons. Nielsen changed its method on September 1, 2025, so 2025 and 2026 figures are not like-for-like.*

q: What drives MLB attendance?

chart.title: Game factors associated with attendance
labels: Games with a closed roof or dome
chart.note: Each bar is compared with its own baseline: Friday for days, August for months, and the average opponent for opponents. Only the largest clear associations are shown.

title: Key drivers of MLB attendance
report: A 69.1% surge in crowds for home openers coincided with the largest attendance gains in Major League Baseball, followed closely by matchups against premium brands like the Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Yankees[1]. Games against the Dodgers coincided with a 25.0% larger crowd, while games against the Yankees were associated with a 15.7% bump[1]. Other opponent matchups coincided with turnout differences ranging from a 6.6% decline for the Miami Marlins to the 25.0% gain for the Dodgers[1]. Scheduling also coincided with turnout variation: compared to Friday games, Saturday dates coincided with an 8.8% rise, while Monday through Thursday games saw drops ranging from 16.6% on Thursdays to 21.8% on Mondays[1]. Summer months also coincided with larger crowds: July games were associated with a 4.2% rise and June games with a 2.5% rise compared to August, while March and April games coincided with a 10.9% drop and May games with a 3.1% decline[1]. Poor weather and stadium conditions also coincided with smaller crowds, as closed roofs or domes were associated with a 7.0% drop and rain, drizzle, or snow with a 5.7% decline[1]. On the field, a win rate worth about 16 more wins in a 162-game season was associated with a 4.7% rise in game attendance and an 8.6% rise in team-season attendance[2]. Finally, a prior two-year crowd that was 10% higher coincided with an 8.2% rise in team average attendance[2]. These patterns are backed by models explaining 82.6% of the variation in game-to-game attendance (n = 7,205 games) and 90.2% of the variation in team-season attendance (n = 86 team-seasons)[3].

q: How did Cubs attendance change by month in 2025?

Friday followed with an average of 32,198 fans (79.7% of capacity), while Sunday averaged 30,949 fans (76.8% of capacity)[2]. Thursday games averaged 28,151 fans (70.2% of capacity)[2]. Tuesday drew an average of 26,644 fans (67.1% of capacity), and Monday averaged 26,397 fans (66.4% of capacity)[2].

sources.query: WITH weekday_stats AS ( SELECT weekday, AVG(attendance) AS avg_attendance, AVG(fill_pct) AS avg_fill_pct FROM games_clean WHERE season = 2025 GROUP BY weekday ) SELECT w1.weekday AS weekday, w1.avg_attendance AS avg_attendance, w1.avg_fill_pct AS avg_fill_pct, w2.weekday AS compare_weekday, w1.avg_attendance - w2.avg_attendance AS attendance_difference, w1.avg_fill_pct - w2.avg_fill_pct AS fill_pct_difference FROM weekday_stats w1 CROSS JOIN weekday_stats w2 ORDER BY w1.weekday, w2.weekday

report: The Los Angeles Dodgers averaged 49,805 fans per game in 2026, which was 1.3% below what the prior two years of crowds, win rate, and market would predict, representing a 0.5% increase of an average of 268 fans per game from the season before[1]. q: Do popular teams explain the link between crowds and TV audiences?
title: MLB attendance and TV audience link
report:
Yes, games with smaller crowds tended to have smaller national TV audiences, but a crowd that was small for its own park did not clearly mean a smaller audience[1]. Comparing games on the same network, the two moved together (correlation 0.34 in 2025, n = 82, range 0.14 to 0.52; 0.47 in 2026, n = 83, range 0.29 to 0.62)[1]. After comparing each game with its own park's usual crowd, the link mostly disappears (0.16 in 2025, range -0.05 to 0.37; 0.14 in 2026, range -0.08 to 0.34; both ranges include zero)[1]. Across team-seasons, teams with bigger average crowds also had bigger average national TV audiences (correlation 0.52, n = 56, range 0.30 to 0.69), which is consistent with team-level factors such as popularity and market size driving both, though the data does not prove the cause[2].

*Viewership figures are publicly reported and may differ from official Nielsen data. They are the national TV audience, excluding streaming add-ons. Nielsen changed its method on September 1, 2025, so 2025 and 2026 figures are not like-for-like.*

q: How much does a team's winning go with higher attendance?
title: Winning percentage and MLB attendance
report: An 8.6% higher season attendance is associated with a team winning about 16 more games over a 162-game season[1]. This team-level relationship comes from a model that explains 90.2% of the differences in attendance among teams ($R^2$ = 0.90, n = 86)[2]. On a game-by-game basis, a win rate worth about 16 more wins in a 162-game season coincides with a 4.7% higher crowd, in a model that accounts for 82.6% of game-by-game attendance variation ($R^2$ = 0.83, n = 7,205)[3][2].

q: How did Yankees national TV audiences change from 2025 to 2026?

chart.title: Average viewers by month, one line per season

title: Yankees national TV audience, 2025 vs 2026
report:
The New York Yankees grew their average national TV audience by 45.9% from 2025 to 2026, jumping by 533,238 viewers, though Nielsen changed its method in September 2025, which generally raised sports audiences[1]. In 2025, the Yankees averaged 1,160,929 viewers across 14 single games with known audiences, out of 14 single games and 19 total appearances, with a peak audience of 2,784,000 viewers[2]. Their 2025 national TV schedule consisted of seven games on TBS, five on ESPN, five on Fox, and two on FS1[2]. In 2026, the Yankees averaged 1,694,167 viewers across 12 single games with known audiences, out of 17 single games and 22 total appearances, peaking at 3,616,000 viewers[2]. Their 2026 network mix expanded to eight games on TBS, five on Fox, three on NBC, two on ESPN, two on FS1, one on ABC, and one on Netflix[2].

*Viewership figures are publicly reported and may differ from official Nielsen data. They are the national TV audience, excluding streaming add-ons.*

sources.query: SELECT v2025.avg_single_game_viewers AS avg_2025, v2026.avg_single_game_viewers AS avg_2026, (v2026.avg_single_game_viewers - v2025.avg_single_game_viewers) AS abs_diff, ROUND(((v2026.avg_single_game_viewers - v2025.avg_single_game_viewers) * 100.0 / v2025.avg_single_game_viewers), 2) AS pct_diff FROM team_tv_summary v2025 JOIN team_tv_summary v2026 ON v2025.team_id = v2026.team_id WHERE v2025.team_id = 147 AND v2025.season = 2025 AND v2026.season = 2026
